question_text: According to the course material, there is no such thing as the exact or univocal definition of philosophy because:
option_a: each philosopher defines philosophy from his or her perspective of its central problem
option_b: every philosopher has already agreed on one official definition
option_c: philosophy is a natural science with laboratory proofs only
option_d: NOUN forbids students from defining the word
explanation: The course material states there is no exact or univocal definition of philosophy; each philosopher defines it from his or her perspective of the central problem or subject matter.

question_text: According to Bodunrin (1981), cited in the course material, a newcomer who wishes to define philosophy is advised to:
option_a: wait, then settle for a definition later in the course of studying philosophy
option_b: memorise one dictionary sentence on the first day
option_c: avoid reading any philosopher until graduation
option_d: treat philosophy as identical with physics
explanation: Bodunrin (1981:12) advises a newcomer wishing to define philosophy to wait and settle for one later in the course of studying philosophy.

question_text: According to the course material, the layman's conception of philosophy simply means:
option_a: the sum of a person's beliefs and the main principles that guide that person's life
option_b: a laboratory method used only by chemists
option_c: the exclusive study of Nigerian criminal statutes
option_d: a prohibition on holding any personal belief
explanation: When we talk of a layman's conception of philosophy, it simply means the sum of a person's beliefs, the main principles that control and guide a person's life.

question_text: According to the course material, the under-labourer conception of philosophy is criticised because:
option_a: it does not capture the sense in which philosophy is understood technically
option_b: it is the only definition every academic accepts
option_c: it proves that philosophy is a branch of accounting
option_d: it forbids any talk of beliefs or world-views
explanation: The material says this impression is under-labourer because it does not capture the sense in which philosophy is understood technically speaking.

question_text: According to the course material, the master-scientist conception of philosophy is inadequate because restricting knowledge to human experience yields:
option_a: half knowledge or lopsided knowledge
option_b: complete knowledge of purpose
explanation: The implication of restricting human knowledge to human experience is half knowledge or lopsided knowledge; reality goes beyond the experimental and observable.

question_text: According to the course material, in the clarification-of-concepts conception, philosophy is reduced to:
option_a: clarifying the meaning of words and concepts such as justice, good, bad, beauty and ugliness
option_b: collecting census data for the federal government
option_c: writing only poetry for commercial prizes
option_d: banning the use of ordinary language
explanation: In this conception, philosophy is reduced to the role of clarification of the meaning of words and concepts such as justice, good, bad, beauty and ugliness.

question_text: According to Harold (1964), cited in the course material, treating clarification as the only legitimate function of philosophy is:
option_a: a narrow conception of philosophy and therefore of knowledge
option_b: the complete and final definition of the discipline
option_c: proof that science cannot yield any knowledge
option_d: identical with Plato's theory of Forms
explanation: To see clarification as the only legitimate function of philosophy is to have a narrow conception of philosophy and therefore of knowledge.

question_text: According to the course material, philosophy as the love of wisdom includes both:
option_a: the seeking of wisdom and the wisdom that is sought
option_b: the rejection of all intellectual effort
option_c: the exclusive pursuit of commercial prizes
option_d: a ban on applying the intellect in daily life
explanation: Philosophy includes both the seeking of wisdom and the wisdom that is sought.

question_text: According to the course material, wisdom in the philosophical sense is distinguished from mere amassed information because:
option_a: one could be wise without much knowledge, just as one could have much knowledge without being wise
option_b: wisdom and knowledge are always identical
option_c: only the uneducated can be wise
explanation: Wisdom is different from, though not opposed to, knowledge as amassed information: one could be wise without much knowledge, and have much knowledge without being wise.

question_text: According to Socrates in the Phaedrus, cited in the course material, a person who can defend his statements when challenged would be called:
option_a: not wise, for that pertains to a god, but a lover of wisdom
option_b: already a god
option_d: a mere copyist of commercial poetry
explanation: Socrates says such a person would be called not wise, for that pertains to a god, but a lover of wisdom (Phaedrus 278d).

question_text: According to the course material, when Leon the tyrant of Phlius asked Pythagoras who he was, Pythagoras replied:
option_a: A philosopher
option_b: A prize-winning athlete
explanation: When Leon the tyrant of Phlius asked him who he was, Pythagoras replied, 'A philosopher'.

question_text: According to Pythagoras, cited via Laertius in the course material, life is compared to the great games where the best people are:
option_a: the spectators, whose interest is the game itself
option_b: those competing only for prizes
option_d: those greedy for fame and gain
explanation: The best were those who went as spectators, since their interest is the game itself; unlike those of servile natures or greedy for fame and gain, the philosopher seeks for truth.

question_text: According to the course material, Plato defines philosophy as:
option_a: a man whose passion is to seek the truth, a man whose heart is fixed on reality
option_b: the exclusive study of market prices
option_c: a refusal to ask any question
explanation: Plato defines philosophy as a man whose passion is to seek the truth, a man whose heart is fixed on reality.

question_text: According to the course material, Aristotle says philosophy is rightly called:
option_a: the knowledge of the truth
option_b: the rejection of all knowledge
explanation: According to Aristotle, philosophy is rightly called the knowledge of the truth.

question_text: According to Omoregbe, with whom the course material submits, philosophy is:
option_a: a rational search for answers to questions that arise when we reflect on human experience
option_b: an irrational refusal to ask questions
option_d: a ban on reflecting on human life
explanation: The material submits with Omoregbe that philosophy is a rational search for answers to the questions that arise in the mind when we reflect on human experience, and a rational search for answers about the ultimate meaning of reality and of human life.

question_text: According to the course material, the Socratic method consists in arguing out the subject in the manner of a:
option_a: dialogue
option_b: silent laboratory experiment only
explanation: The Socratic method consists in arguing out the entire process of the subject in question, in the manner of a dialogue.

question_text: According to the course material, Socratic irony is:
option_a: the assumption of an ignorance of truth by the teacher
option_b: the teacher's claim to already know every truth
option_c: a refusal to ask any question
option_d: the use of only written lectures
explanation: The method can be summed up including: the assumption of an ignorance of truth by the teacher, which has been called the Socratic irony.

question_text: According to the course material, Socratic questioning that brings knowledge to the surface is often called:
option_a: the art of philosophic midwifery
option_b: algebraic substitution
explanation: This common ground of truth among men can be brought out by careful analysis, argument and investigation, by question and answer. This is often called the art of philosophic midwifery.

question_text: According to the course material, the Socratic method is also described as adopting:
option_a: the inductive method of reasoning, proceeding from observed facts to more general truths
option_b: only guesswork with no reasoning
option_d: the exclusive use of laboratory chemicals
explanation: The art of proceeding from the observed facts to more general truths, i.e., adopting the inductive method of reasoning.

question_text: According to the course material, Unit 2 of Module 1 examines methods of philosophy beginning from:
option_a: the time of Socrates
option_b: the founding of NOUN in 2002
explanation: You shall be examining the various ways by which philosophical processes have been carried out from the time of Socrates.

question_text: According to the course material, the major branches of philosophy treated in Module 1 Unit 3 are:
option_a: Logic, Metaphysics, Epistemology and Ethics
option_b: Accounting, Marketing, Banking and Tourism
explanation: The unit contents list Logic, Metaphysics, Epistemology and Ethics as the major branches.

question_text: According to Copi, cited in the course material, logic is:
option_a: the study of the methods and principles used in distinguishing good (correct) from bad (incorrect) reasoning
option_b: the study of plant taxonomy only
explanation: Copi defines logic as the study of the methods and principles used in distinguishing good (correct) from bad (incorrect) reasoning (1972).

question_text: According to the course material, etymologically logic as a discipline derives from the Greek word Logos, which means:
option_a: Reasoned discourse
option_b: Market price
explanation: Etymologically, logic as a discipline derives from the Greek word Logos, which means Reasoned discourse.

question_text: According to the course material, logic is described as:
option_a: an instrumental branch of philosophy and the tool of philosophizing
option_b: a replacement for all other branches of philosophy
explanation: Logic is an instrumental branch of philosophy. In point of fact, always remember that logic is the tool of philosophizing.

question_text: According to the course material, besides the four traditional branches, other branches are often referred to as:
option_a: the philosophy of the infrastructure of disciplines
option_b: the abolition of all other subjects
explanation: There are other branches of philosophy which are often referred to as the philosophy of the infrastructure of disciplines.

question_text: According to the course material, Module 1 Unit 4 focuses specifically on the relationship between philosophy and:
option_a: the sciences, religion, education and law
option_b: football, music, fashion and cooking only
explanation: The focus in this unit will be specifically on the relationship between philosophy, the sciences, religion, education and law.

question_text: According to the course material, some people see no relevance in philosophy because they conceive it as:
option_a: an abstract contemplation far removed from practical living
option_b: a purely vocational trade
explanation: Those who conceive philosophy as intellectually complex and as an abstract contemplation far removed from practical living do not see any meaningfulness or relevance in philosophical enterprise.

question_text: According to the course material, the sources of knowledge emphasised in Module 1 Unit 6 include reason, sense experience, intuition, authority, and:
option_a: revelation and faith
option_b: soil pH readings only
explanation: The unit contents list sources of knowledge as reason, sense experience, intuition, authority, and revelation and faith.

question_text: According to the course material, in common-sense usage knowledge, opinion and belief are often:
option_a: used interchangeably
option_b: strictly distinguished by every layman
explanation: Often knowledge, opinion and belief are used interchangeably. This confusion mostly appears in common sense usage.

question_text: According to the course material, knowing a great deal about Plato without having met him shows that:
option_a: one can know a great deal about a person one has never met
option_b: knowledge always requires personal acquaintance
option_c: Plato cannot be studied at NOUN
option_d: belief and knowledge are the same
explanation: As a student of philosophy, you know a great deal about Plato, but I am sure that you never met him.
